chapter: Early years with Paul Barnes and King Oliver
title: Meeting Paul Barnes in 1929, the Homer band, and joining King Oliver
summary: Reason tells how he met Barnes in New Iberia while with the Nighthawks, played with Barnes's band in Homer, Louisiana, then followed Barnes to King Oliver's band after the bus burned.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: When did you first meet Paul? I met Paul in 1929 in New Iberia, Louisiana. I was playing with a band under the leadership of Beauregard Adams, an alto player. And the name of the band was the Nighthawks, a six-piece band. And during that time, times were pretty tough. So we were working on these $2, $2.50, $3.00 night jobs. And I had been with them about a year. And I knew the whole territory by going around with this little band. And, in fact, I came to New Iberia on a freight train. It was during the Depression, and everybody traveled around on a freight train. And Paul D. Barnes had a band with Nellie Lutcher and Kermit Scott and Elris Joseph, a drummer, and quite a few others. I can't recall their names right now. Their bass player, Chester, lived in New Orleans, now has no Chester's last name. And they had a big band. In fact, they had one of the best bands in the whole territory. But they couldn't find work because they were playing special arrangements. And that Creole session down there hadn't begun to understand what special arrangements were. And Paul D. Barnes was writing the arrangements. And he and I became friends. And he asked me to come go with them on a few jobs. And I went with them and showed them different places at Sheraton Beach, around Generate, different places around where they could meet with different dance hall owners. And I went with them. At that time, there weren't too much dealings with night clubs. It was mostly dance halls. And I went with them. And when they got ready to leave, it was around the carnival season, the Lenten season. And most of the fellas in Paul D. Barnes band went back to Lake Charles, the home of Nelly Lecher, pianist. And I went along with Paul D. Barnes to Homer, Louisiana. And a man by the name of Vincent Lepresto had a jitney dance place. This hall was in Homer, Louisiana. And he talked with Paul D. Barnes. We had played there a couple of times. Paul was about the most popular band leader out in this territory at that time. And Paul went to New Orleans and we got D.D. Pierce. His name is Joseph Pierce. We called him D.D. The trumpet player, Euless Jean, which is trumpet. And we had a drummer that used to be with Sidney Desfene. We called him Shine. Nolan Williams is his right name. Paul was playing alto sax. And he got another saxophone player from Idaho, who is also deceased now. My name is Sammy Johnson. And we started to play on Wednesdays and Saturday nights in Homer. And we'd play on Sunday nights for the American Legion. And Monday nights we'd play spot dance jobs around Morgan City, Thibodeau. And even we went back as far as New Iberia and played dance. We had a smaller band then, but we played more stock arrangements and head arrangements instead of the organized special arrangements. And we stayed there. In fact, Paul stayed there about a year. And he went back with King Oliver's band. That was early thirties. And he joined King Oliver's band. Let me see, they were in Huntington, West Virginia. And after being there, about a couple of months, he told King Oliver about me. And I had met Louis Armstrong in New Orleans, but he didn't know too much about me. And Paul joined King Oliver's band. And they were working in Portsmouth, Ohio. That's where King Oliver's bus burned up. And over half of the musicians quit King. And Charlie Turan was the pianist. And he quit and married a woman who had seven children in Portsmouth. And he quit the music game. And just started working around Portsmouth. Very good musician. And they sent for me. And I kept the telegram about four weeks. I didn't know how to leave Louisiana. I had never gone out of Louisiana in my life. And so we had, after I received the telegram, they sent it to New Orleans, then they forwarded it to home Louisiana. And I met with Professor Ernie, who has a music store. He's now retired in Lafayette, Louisiana. He had a band, and he was also teaching bands in different public schools. And I showed it to him, and he and I were very good friends. And he said to me, he said, man, you can always come back to Louisiana and make three dollars a night. He said, this is a good experience for you. And I said, well, I think I'll do that. I was teaching music in Homer, Louisiana at that time and playing with the rest of the band after Paul left. Because we were making more money even at that time, the three and four dollars a night, than the musicians around New Orleans were making. And I left. And I went with King Oliver, and I stayed with him about three years. Then Paul left first, and came back home. And a little later on, the band was just about going down. And I left the band, came back to New Orleans. And I got a job working at the same night. I just went by the same bass player. I was trying to call his name a while ago, Chester's Chester's Artist. I think that's the name.
